lesson_title: Why One Blown Bulb Does Not Black Out Your House
hook_text: The kitchen bulb blows, but the lounge light stays on. That is the magic of parallel circuits.
clip_script: When a bulb blows in your kitchen, the lounge light stays on. That is because your home is wired in parallel. The wire splits into separate branches, and each light sits on its own complete loop. Three rules. One: every branch gets the full voltage, so each bulb shines just as brightly as it would alone. Two: the current splits at every junction and adds back up when the branches meet. If 0,5 amperes leaves the battery and one branch takes 0,2, the other takes 0,3. Three: every extra branch is another path, like opening another till at the supermarket, so the total resistance goes down and the total current goes up. That is the danger: switch on the kettle, heater, iron and toaster on one circuit and the current can overload the wiring. That is why your distribution board has circuit breakers waiting to trip.
visual_style: A house cutaway with lights on separate branches; one bulb blowing while others glow; animated current splitting and rejoining; supermarket tills opening; a circuit breaker tripping.
pacing: Domestic hook, three crisp rules, a building tension with appliances, a click of the breaker to finish.
